```{r setup, include = FALSE}

```

inlabru practitioners often evaluate models by how well their posterior
predictive distribution covers held-out data, rather than by point-forecast
error alone. A scoring rule is *proper* if it is minimised in expectation only
when the forecaster reports their true predictive distribution — this rules out
gaming by sharpening or widening predictions artificially.

inlaops provides `bru_score()` to compute four scores using the full posterior
predictive distribution via `inlabru::generate()` and the `scoringRules`
package. CRPS and log-score are strictly proper. Squared error evaluates only
the posterior mean. Dawid-Sebastiani is proper for location-scale families.

## Setup

```{r}
library(inlabru)
library(inlaops)
library(scoringRules)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## The four scores

| Score | Formula | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| CRPS | $\text{E}[\|X - y\|] - \frac{1}{2}\text{E}[\|X - X'\|]$ | Lower is better. Generalises MAE. Works for any distribution. |
| Log-score | $-\log p(y)$ | Lower is better. Penalises overconfident wrong predictions heavily. |
| SE | $(y - \hat{\mu})^2$ | Squared error of the posterior mean. |
| Dawid-Sebastiani | $\frac{(y - \hat{\mu})^2}{\hat{\sigma}^2} + \log \hat{\sigma}^2$ | Penalises miscalibrated variance. |

CRPS and log-score are fully proper — they evaluate the entire predictive
distribution, not just the mean or variance. SE only assesses the posterior
mean and ignores predictive uncertainty. Dawid-Sebastiani is a Gaussian
approximation to the log-score.

## Example: comparing two models

```{r}
set.seed(42)
n   <- 500
dat <- data.frame(
  x1 = rnorm(n),
  x2 = rnorm(n),
  x3 = rnorm(n)
)
dat$y <- 1.5 + 0.9 * dat$x1 + 0.3 * dat$x2 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.8)

# Hold out 20% for evaluation
idx_holdout <- sample(n, size = 100L)
train_dat   <- dat[-idx_holdout, ]
test_dat    <- dat[ idx_holdout, ]
```

Fit two models: a correctly-specified model and a model that omits `x2`.

```{r}
fit_full <- bru(
  y ~ Intercept(1) + x1 + x2,
  family  = "gaussian",
  data    = train_dat,
  options = bru_options(control.compute = list(config = TRUE))
)

fit_reduced <- bru(
  y ~ Intercept(1) + x1,
  family  = "gaussian",
  data    = train_dat,
  options = bru_options(control.compute = list(config = TRUE))
)
```

Score both models against the holdout set. `bru_score()` calls
`inlabru::generate()` to draw raw posterior samples and passes them to
`scoringRules`.

The prediction formula must produce samples of **Y**, including the
observation-model stochasticity. The package is family-agnostic — you write
the appropriate `r*()` call yourself. Inside an `inlabru::generate()`
formula the predictor is evaluated once per posterior sample: latent-field
symbols (`Intercept`, `field`, ...) are scalars per sample, and covariates
(`x1`, `x2`) are vectors over observations. So `length(<covariate>)` is
the per-sample observation count for the `r*()` call:

For continuous families the SD has to come from outside the predictor
formula. inlabru's `generate()` evaluator exposes latent-field samples
(`Intercept`, fixed effects, SPDE) and `newdata` columns, but **not**
hyperparameter samples by symbol — the precision hyperparameter is
unavailable inside the formula. Two pragmatic options:

1. **Use a known SD** — the simulation truth, a prior summary, or the
   posterior-mean SD computed offline (`1 / sqrt(fit$summary.hyperpar["Precision for the Gaussian observations", "mean"])`).
   Simple, slightly under-states predictive variance because it ignores
   posterior uncertainty in the precision itself.
2. **Hand-roll the scoring** — draw latent and hyperparameter samples
   together via `INLA::inla.posterior.sample()`, combine, and call
   `scoringRules` directly. More rigorous; about 15 lines of code.
   See the optional section below.

For this toy the truth is `sd = 0.8` (the value we used to simulate
`dat$y`):

```{r}
scores_full <- bru_score(
  fit_full,
  newdata      = test_dat,
  pred_formula = ~ rnorm(
    length(x1), mean = Intercept + x1 + x2,
    sd   = 0.8
  ),
  y_col        = "y",
  n_samples    = 2000L
)

scores_reduced <- bru_score(
  fit_reduced,
  newdata      = test_dat,
  pred_formula = ~ rnorm(
    length(x1), mean = Intercept + x1,
    sd   = 0.8
  ),
  y_col        = "y",
  n_samples    = 2000L
)
```

Dropping the `rnorm(...)` layer would make `bru_score()` compute CRPS and
log-score against draws of the *posterior mean* — understating predictive
variance and yielding optimistic scores.

### Optional — hand-rolled scoring with posterior precision

If you need to integrate over posterior uncertainty in the Gaussian
precision rather than fixing the SD, draw joint posterior samples via
`INLA::inla.posterior.sample()` and combine them yourself:

```{r}
post <- INLA::inla.posterior.sample(
  n      = 2000L,
  result = fit_full,
  add.names = FALSE
)

# Per-sample Gaussian precision and SD.
prec <- vapply(post, function(s) {
  s$hyperpar["Precision for the Gaussian observations"]
}, numeric(1))
sd_samples <- 1 / sqrt(prec)

# Per-sample linear predictor at the holdout points. inlabru::generate()
# returns one row per observation, one column per sample.
mu_samples <- inlabru::generate(
  fit_full,
  newdata   = test_dat,
  formula   = ~ Intercept + x1 + x2,
  n.samples = 2000L
)

# Add observation noise per (obs, sample) cell. sd_samples is recycled
# across rows.
y_samples <- mu_samples + matrix(
  rnorm(length(mu_samples), sd = sd_samples),
  nrow = nrow(mu_samples), byrow = TRUE
)

scoringRules::crps_sample(test_dat$y, y_samples)
scoringRules::logs_sample(test_dat$y, y_samples)
```

The `inlabru::generate()` and `INLA::inla.posterior.sample()` calls draw
from the same posterior but use independent sampler runs — for
fully-coupled (latent, hyperparameter) draws you need to build both from
a single `inla.posterior.sample()` invocation. That is overkill for
exploratory scoring; the independent-draw approximation is fine in
practice.

Summarise mean scores across holdout observations:

```{r}
bind_rows(
  mutate(scores_full,    model = "full"),
  mutate(scores_reduced, model = "reduced")
) |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(
    mean_crps = mean(crps),
    mean_logs = mean(logs),
    mean_rmse = sqrt(mean(se))
  )
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   model   mean_crps mean_logs mean_rmse
#>   <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 full        0.452     1.031     0.799
#> 2 reduced     0.491     1.097     0.857
```

The full model scores better on all three metrics.

## Visualising score distributions

Mean scores can hide important heterogeneity. Plot the per-observation score
distributions to identify systematic patterns:

```{r}
bind_rows(
  mutate(scores_full,    model = "full"),
  mutate(scores_reduced, model = "reduced")
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = crps, fill = model)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "CRPS (lower is better)", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Observations where the reduced model scores much worse than the full model are
precisely those with large `x2` values — confirming that omitting `x2` hurts
predictions at the tails.

## Relationship to WAIC and DIC

WAIC and DIC are information criteria computed on the training data. Proper
scoring rules are computed against genuinely held-out observations.

| Metric | Computed on | Accounts for overfitting? | Available at serving time? |
|---|---|---|---|
| DIC | Training | Via effective parameters | No — pin metadata only |
| WAIC | Training | More reliably than DIC | No — pin metadata only |
| CRPS / log-score | Holdout | Yes | Via `bru_score()` |

Use WAIC/DIC for fast model selection during development (no holdout needed).
Use CRPS/log-score for final model comparison and reporting. Both are stored in
`glance_bru()`:

```{r}
glance(fit_full)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>     dic   waic marginal_loglik  nobs elapsed
#>   <dbl>  <dbl>           <dbl> <int>   <dbl>
#> 1  812.   815.           -408.   400    0.63
```

## Scoring spatial and non-Gaussian models

The contract is the same for spatial and non-spatial fits: `pred_formula`
must produce samples of `Y`. The package does not inject family-aware
observation noise — write the appropriate `r*()` call.

The blocks below are **illustrative API sketches**, not runnable end-to-end
(they reference `spatial_fit`, `poisson_fit`, etc. — substitute your own
fitted model). They show the formula shape per family:

```r
# Spatial Gaussian model with SPDE field
spatial_scores <- bru_score(
  spatial_fit,
  newdata      = holdout_sp,              # SpatialPointsDataFrame or sf
  pred_formula = ~ rnorm(
    length(x1), mean = Intercept + field,
    sd   = 1 / sqrt(precision_for_the_gaussian_observations)
  ),
  y_col        = "y",
  n_samples    = 1000L
)

# Poisson — write the rpois yourself.
poisson_scores <- bru_score(
  poisson_fit,
  newdata      = holdout_sp,
  pred_formula = ~ rpois(length(x1), exp(Intercept + field)),
  y_col        = "counts",
  n_samples    = 1000L
)

# Binomial — pass the trial count via newdata column (e.g. `trials`).
# Inside the formula, covariate columns are vectors so `trials` and
# `length(trials)` both work.
binomial_scores <- bru_score(
  binomial_fit,
  newdata      = holdout_sp,
  pred_formula = ~ rbinom(
    length(trials), size = trials,
    prob = plogis(Intercept + field)
  ),
  y_col        = "successes",
  n_samples    = 1000L
)

# Negative binomial — INLA's nbinomial parameterisation uses size on the
# precision scale; check your fit's hyperparameter names. A simpler path
# when you don't want to bake INLA's hyperpar names into the formula is
# to score on a known approximate dispersion:
nb_scores <- bru_score(
  nb_fit,
  newdata      = holdout_sp,
  pred_formula = ~ rnbinom(
    length(x1), mu = exp(Intercept + field),
    size = known_size
  ),
  y_col        = "counts",
  n_samples    = 1000L
)
```

For zero-inflated families, sample the mixture explicitly:
`ifelse(runif(length(x), ...) < pi, 0, rpois(length(x), lambda))`.

## Notes on `n_samples`

`bru_score()` uses `inlabru::generate()` which draws from the full joint
posterior via `inla.posterior.sample()`. Increasing `n_samples` reduces Monte
Carlo variance in the scores at the cost of computation time.

- For development and model comparison: 500–1000 samples is usually sufficient.
- For final evaluation and reporting: 2000–5000 samples.
- CRPS converges faster than log-score, which requires accurate tail
  probability estimates.
